# Assumptions (generated by tools/assumptions.py; do not edit by hand)

Basis labels: DATA (measured), LITERATURE (cited), DECISION (author), JUDGEMENT (not identifiable from data; bracketed by sensitivities in outputs/data/baseline/sensitivity_one_at_a_time.csv).

### Limitation of the 2026 overbuild rule

- The vacancy-rate parameter is held at its published 2023 census value (5.39%; on the consistent definition 2023 is the series maximum, 5.38%, minimum 4.01% in 1996); implied stock vacancy rises to ≈6.4% because the 2026 overbuild is not absorbed. The 2026 overbuild (≈27,500 dwellings over 2026-2050, of which ≈24,600 in 2026-2028) is not absorbed by later demand, so the implied stock vacancy stays about 1 percentage point above the 1986-2023 range on a consistent definition (4.0-5.4%). Absorption is not modelled: the persistence rho = 0.52 (lag-1 autocorrelation of the annual departure of building from the calibrated stock identity, 1992-2023) describes how a flow deviation fades (already used for the excess), not a payback of the stock, and the eight census vacancy observations do not identify a mean-reversion rate.

### Limitations of the material decarbonisation

- Decarbonisation paths are relative changes for European and global market processes modelled with premise on ecoinvent 3.9.1 (Horup et al. 2025); they are applied as relative changes to New Zealand case-study factors. This assumes NZ material supply decarbonises at the same relative rate as those markets, which is not tested.
- Items without a counterpart in Horup et al. follow a labelled proxy path (polymers, paint and SIP at EPS, the smallest reduction in the set; gypsum plasterboard at clay brick) or are held at 2025 (the lift); the proxies are a judgement, bracketed by holding them at 2025 (sensitivity).
- C1-C4 (end of life) is held at 2025 factors (no source for end-of-life decarbonisation); future end-of-life technology would lower the committed emissions (conservative).
- Horup et al. (2025) SI Table S4 gives the average of the 9 premise scenarios only; the scenario range is shown graphically in their Fig. 2, so no low/high decarbonisation path is implemented.
- Several items are made in New Zealand with electricity-intensive production (aluminium, Pink Batts glass wool, Pacific Steel rebar, WPMA Radiata timber, Nelson Pine LVL); the aluminium items are stated in their EPD names to use mainly renewables-generated electricity. Where their 2025 factors already reflect low-carbon electricity, the premise paths, which include the decarbonisation of electricity supply ("The Premise software accounts for future changes in several critical sectors (supply of conventional and alternative fuels, electricity, cement and steel production and freight and passenger road transportation), and includes implementation of technologies such as carbon capture and storage in steel and cement production" (Horup et al. 2025, p. 5)), may overstate their relative reduction; a sensitivity holds them at 2025.
- Composite floor decking (an RC item containing its steel deck and rebar) follows the concrete-structure path because the source gives no split; this is conservative versus steel profile for the steel share.

### Limitations of the time-resolved accounting and the A4-A5 path

- Event timing is deterministic (n events evenly spaced in the building life). Resch et al. (2021, Section 2.2 and Fig. 4) model replacement years as probability-distributed; the L / n sensitivity brackets the timing within the service-life range implied by the counts, but not early or late failures.
- A4-A5 follows a generic technological-progress factor (Resch et al. 2021, Table 1) because it cannot be separated by material process; Horup et al. (2025, Fig. 2A, pp. 5-6) show that generic factors oversimplify material-specific trends, and Resch et al. state that "the decay functions should not be interpreted as predictions" (p. 4). Sensitivities: held at 2025 and the item S4 paths.
- Emissions committed after 2050 (later B2/B4 and C1-C4) are a range bounded by two conventions (2025 factors; the 2050 factors held), not a projection: the source paths end in 2050 and C1-C4 has no decarbonisation source.
- The repaint composition differs from the first coat but cannot be separated in the source file; repaints take the line's initial stage split (negligible: the paint path is the EPS proxy).
- Completion rate 0.95: "Jones et al. 2024" is a citation to verify (TODO: confirm the reference before submission).

### Other limitations of the projection

- No national demolition data: demolition of detached buildings up to three storeys is consent-exempt, so the implied replacement rates cannot be tested against a count.
- N4 (open): the Low/High household-size variants (deterministic) are paired with stochastic population percentiles through one draw z, and the total vs private-household population question is unresolved until the living-arrangement table (E2); the household projections are 2018-base, with Stats NZ's 2023-base release (late 2026) to be adopted in a later version.
- Timber end of life (C1-C4) excludes biogenic CO2 (confirmed by the author). Whether it includes landfill methane is TO CONFIRM from Christoforatos & Pickering 2025 (author check).
- With the typology mix held in every variant (internal to the model: it weights the case-study factors), neither the variants nor the Monte Carlo carry typology-mix uncertainty; a change of mix is a pathway question for later work, not a baseline uncertainty.
- The soil factor was derived for Auckland's future urban zones and is applied nationally.
- The case-study carbon factor for apartments rests on one independent case study (A_1 and A_2 are one design at two scales).
- The regional analysis of the recent replacement surge (replacement half-life by territorial authority) is deferred.
- Net replacement persistence (the replacement half-life of the Reference) is not identifiable from the census record; Low replacement and High replacement bound it.
- The 2018 census empty-dwelling count has no quality rating (DataInfo+); the vacancy terms rely on it.
- The 2026 overbuild fades at the persistence estimated on the calibrated stock identity (rho), not on market cycles (an assumption).
- W from Little's law is a lower bound on the completion lag.
- Retirement-village floor area is reported but out of carbon scope.

### Limitations of the planetary-boundary layer (AESA)

- Static carrying capacity: the carrying capacities are constant yearly values modelled at steady state and their timespan may not match the assessment period (Clausen et al. 2025, pp. 143 and 148).
- Accounting (time-resolved): the sector impact of 2026-2050 counts materials and construction (A1-A5) and soil carbon loss in the construction year and maintenance (B2, B4) in the year it occurs. Maintenance after 2050 and all end-of-life emissions (C1-C4) of the 2026-2050 cohorts are committed after 2050, outside 2026-2050; they are reported as a range (outputs/data/aesa/results.json "committed", Fig3c) in years of the 2050 AR boundary and are not compared with the 2026-2050 boundary. Whole life at construction is a sensitivity.
- History at 2025 factors: the acquired-rights base (2016-2025) and the base-window sensitivities use the 2025 case-study factors because no historical factor series exists for the case studies. If past production was more carbon-intensive than in 2025 (as the ~1%/yr technological progress assumed by Resch et al. 2021 implies), the base and hence the AR boundary are understated and the AR exceedance overstated (conservative); the size of this effect is not quantified. The base follows the projection's accounting rule (materials and construction and soil carbon loss of the base window's construction plus the maintenance within the base window of the cohorts built in it).
- The primary SOS (6.81E12) is the 2 °C carrying capacity of Bjørn & Hauschild (2015), not the 1 W/m² planetary boundary (3.61E12, sensitivity C). Sala et al. (2020, Table 3) label 6.81E12 as radiative forcing after Rockström et al. (2009), which does not match its derivation in Bjørn & Hauschild (2015).
- GWP basis: Bjørn & Hauschild (2015) ESM2 uses AR5 GWP100 factors (CH4 28, N2O 265; column "CFs (GWP100, IPCC5)") while their Table 1 cites Forster et al. (2007), i.e. AR4. The GWP basis of the case-study LCA factors used by the model is not documented in this repository (building_data.xlsx gives "GWP" columns only; source Christoforatos & Pickering 2025): to be confirmed by the author.
- I_glob = 5.58E13 (Bjørn & Hauschild 2015 ESM2, from Laurent et al. 2013, year 2010): Laurent et al. (2013) is not in hand, so whether it includes land-use-change CO2 (the sector impact includes soil carbon loss) and its GWP basis are NOT VERIFIED. The per-gas indicator scores in ESM2 sum to 54.0 Gt CO2-eq with 39.5 Gt CO2; a CO2 total of that size is consistent with inclusion of land-use-change CO2 (inference, not a sourced statement). The EC-JRC table "Normalization factors for testing" (Benini, Sala & Pant, version 0.1.1, 15 Dec 2015; sheet 1.3) gives the PROSUITE global value as 5.589E13 kg CO2-eq, 8,100 kg/person, "2010 or 2000".
- Final-consumption-expenditure upscaling: the numerator (consented residential value) is an investment flow (gross fixed capital formation), while Hjalsted et al. (2021) define the upscaling on final consumption and leave intermediate sectors as open (p. 16).
- Ability to pay: Hjalsted et al. (2021) state GDP as "USD/cap (2017)", World Bank (2019), without naming the series; current US$ is the sensitivity. The GDP coverage excludes economies without the measure (listed in outputs/data/aesa/results.json).
- Monte Carlo: I_sec,base is recomputed in every draw with that draw's case-study carbon factors (2025 technology), so the factor uncertainty is treated alike in the base and the projection; it does not co-vary with the draw's completion rate or dwelling size (historical floor area is observed).
- The numerical results in Hjalsted et al.'s SI (Tables S4-S9) are reproduced only with α = 1; we apply α as specified in their Eq. 5 and SI Eq. S1, which ensures national shares sum to the global SOS. The authors have been contacted.

## Pathways (levers.py, pathways.py)

Resolved values from outputs/data/pathways/levers.json and, for the theoretical limit TL, outputs/data/pathways/theoretical_limit.json; Table 1 of the paper: outputs/reports/LEVERS_TABLE.md; methods as implemented: outputs/reports/METHODS_DRAFT.md (3. Pathways and the theoretical limit).

| setting | value | basis |
|---|---|---|
| Pathways | P1 Space per person (L1 Dwelling size + L2 Household occupancy), P2 Existing stock (L3 Vacancy + L4 Overbuild absorption + L5 Building lifetime extension), P3 Construction (L6 Material carbon + L7 Construction-stage carbon), P4 Land (L8 Soil-aware planning + L9 Brownfield development), P5 Combined (every lever); settings Moderate (headline) and Ambitious (sensitivity); Reference projection, with the Low and High replacement variants for the Reference and P5; only Population growth is untargeted | DECISION (author) |
| Adoption path | normalised logistic s(y) = 1 / (1 + exp(-k (y - 2030.5))), k = ln(81)/6 = 0.7324; w = (s(y) - s(2026)) / (s(2035) - s(2026)), 1 after 2035, 0 up to 2026 (full roll-out by 2035, adopted); one rule for every window 2026 -> E (W = E - 2026): midpoint 2026 + W/2, k = ln(81) / (2W/3); sensitivities (P5): full roll-out by 2030 (midpoint 2028, k = 1.6479) and by 2045 (midpoint 2035.5, k = 0.3469) | LITERATURE: full roll-out by 2035 following RECC (Pauliuk et al. 2024, J. Ind. Ecol. 28, 1699: circular-economy strategies fully implemented by 2035); DECISION (author): the logistic form |
| Business-as-usual decarbonisation | applies in every run (A1-A3 item paths of Horup et al. 2025; A4-A5 e^(-0.01 (t - 2025)), the reference path of L7) | LITERATURE |
| Typology mix | Reference (held) shares in every run; The denser typology mix (lever of pathways_v2, removed in pathways_v3.1) was not carried forward: within the embodied-carbon scope a denser mix raises A1-A3 per m2 (attached typologies carry more per m2), while its benefits (infrastructure, operational energy, land) are outside the scope. Values from git tag pathways_v2 (Reference): Moderate / Ambitious carbon -0.39% / -2.94% vs the Reference | DECISION (author); DATA: git tag pathways_v2 |
| 2026 overbuild under the levers | held at the Reference path (dwellings) in every run except L4; the overbuild is the observed 2026 pipeline, not demand | DECISION (author) |
| Vacancy check | implied vacancy 1 - hh / physical stock >= 4.0% in every year of every pathway run | DECISION (author) |
| Attribution | Shapley values (Shapley 1953; Albrecht, Francois & Schoors 2002, Energy Policy 30, 727) over the 16 pathway subsets (main) and the 512 lever subsets (SI), exact rational arithmetic, on cumulative carbon and cumulative LoE AR; demand bands give the attribution by band exactly | LITERATURE; DECISION (author) |
| Back-cast | uniform factor k on the floor area of every 2027-2050 cohort of P5 and the Reference (2026 fixed), brentq for cumulative LoE AR = 1; AtP: minimum LoE at k = 0 | DECISION (author) |
| Solution space | uniform cuts of 2027-2050 floor area and of non-soil carbon per m2 of the 2027-2050 cohorts, 0-100% in 5% steps, applied to the Reference | LITERATURE: Horup et al. 2025, Sci. Total Environ. 966, 178780, Fig. 6 (form); DECISION (author) |

(2024) Building and Environment 256, 111505, Table 2 (individual dwellings 107 -> 100 m2, -6.5%); Pauliuk S, et al. (2024) Building and Environment 256, 111505 (demolition 150,000 -> 90,000 a year, -40%) |

| Omitted: Bio-based archetypes | not modelled | DECISION (author): no typology has a bio-based archetype among the 16 case studies, and the model's biogenic-carbon convention (timber C1-C4 excludes biogenic CO2) would need extending; overlaps L6 |
| Omitted: Renovation carbon of retained buildings | not modelled | DECISION (author): not modelled: L5 is an upper bound of the effect of building lifetime extension (Napiontek et al. 2025) |
| Theoretical limit TL | TL is a hyper-optimistic theoretical limit; a thought experiment, not a pathway: every lever at its limit, adopted by 2030, combining best observed attributes of different buildings and places; not a proposal or a feasible pathway (potentials hierarchy: theoretical > technical > realisable). TL = P5 Combined (Moderate) with TL1-TL10, every lever and item on the standard adoption rule with full roll-out by 2030 (logistic, midpoint 2028, k = ln(81) / (8/3) = 1.6479; the window of the pathways' 2030 sensitivity); 2026 untouched; every TL item at least as strong as the Ambitious setting of its lever (asserted). Released dwellings (zero vacancy, the household-size change, the 2026 overbuild) re-occupied at a constant share of each year's need 2027-2050. Sensitivity: every limit at full strength from 1 January 2027 (instant, same rule). The adopted decarbonisation applies in TL as in every run (A1-A3 item paths of Horup et al. 2025; A4-A5 e^(-0.01 (t - 2025)) until TL7 sets A4-A5 to zero). | DECISION (author) |
| TL1 No extra space | f = 1; how: L1 with f = 1: new-dwelling size = occupied area S x OLF; vs Ambitious: f = 0.5 | DECISION (author): limit of L1 |

| TL3 No vacancy | v = 0; how: v = 0 by 2030; the dwellings released are re-occupied at a constant share s = min(R, G+) / G+ of each year's need, never ahead of the cumulative release; vs Ambitious: v* = 0.04 | DECISION (author): limit of L3 |
| TL4 Overbuild fully absorbed | a = 1; how: the 2026 overbuild absorbed in full from 2027 (absorption 1; L4 / TL4 act through the absorption rate, not the adoption path); vs Ambitious: a = 0.2 | DECISION (author): limit of L4 |
| TL5 Building lifetime extension at the limit | d = 0.40 (demolition); surge removed; how: demolition x (1 - 0.40); the recent replacement surge removed (replacement at the long-run 1991-2023 rate, as the Low variant); vs Ambitious: d = 0.4 (both) | LITERATURE + DATA: LITERATURE: Pellan2024; DATA: the long-run census rate |
